title: remember, state hoisting, saveable
scopeHtml: Scope: remember and keys, rememberSaveable and Savers, state hoisting and state holders, derivedStateOf, snapshotFlow, collectAsStateWithLifecycle, stale captures. Recomposition scopes and snapshot internals are in R1; effect handlers are in E1; UDF architecture is A4; process death mechanics are A2.

questions.promptHtml: What does remember do, and what is the difference between val x = 0, val x = remember { 0 } and val x = remember { mutableStateOf(0) } inside a composable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you separate "survives recomposition" from "triggers recomposition". Most 3-YOE answers blur the two.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A composable re-executes on every recomposition, so a plain local is re-initialised each time. remember stores the lambda's result in the composition's slot table and returns the stored value on later passes. It does not make anything observable. mutableStateOf makes the value observable so writes schedule recomposition. You almost always need both: remember { mutableStateOf(..) }."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• remember is positional memoization. The compiler gives each call site a group key. On first composition the lambda runs and the result is written into the slot table at that position. On recomposition remember reads that slot back.
  • The value lives until the call site leaves the composition (the if branch goes false, the item is removed, the whole host is disposed). Configuration change destroys the composition, so the value is lost (that is what rememberSaveable is for).
  • Observability is a separate mechanism: MutableState is a snapshot state object. Reads inside composition are tracked and writes invalidate those reads.
Declaration Survives recomposition Write triggers recomposition
val x = 0 No (reset each pass) n/a
val x = remember { 0 } Yes n/a (immutable)
val x = remember { mutableStateOf(0) } Yes Yes
val x = remember { mutableListOf<Int>() } Yes No (not observable)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Counter() {
    var count by remember { mutableIntStateOf(0) } // survives + observable
    var lost = 0                                   // resets on every recomposition
    Button(onClick = { count++; lost++ }) { Text("count=$count lost=$lost") }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• remember { mutableListOf() } and then .add(): value survives but UI never updates (use mutableStateListOf).
  • Using remember to hold something that must survive rotation.
  • Thinking remember is a cache shared across call sites: it is per position in the tree, not per type or per name.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where is the value stored? → In the slot table of the Composition, at the position of the call site.
  2. Is remember thread-safe? → No guarantee; the lambda runs on the composing thread and must not be used for shared mutable state.
  3. What happens if the same composable is called twice in a Column? → Two call-site instances of its body give two independent slots, because position in the group tree differs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "remember keeps state across recompositions." Senior: separates memoization from observability, names the slot table and positional identity, and explains when the stored value is dropped (leaves composition, key changes).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A remember { mutableListOf() } in a cart screen "worked" in debug because something else forced recomposition; in release the UI lagged one action behind.

questions.promptHtml: How do keys passed to remember work, and when do you need them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Stale cached values after an input changes are a classic Compose bug.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Keys are the inputs the calculation depends on. On each recomposition remember compares the new keys to the stored ones using equals; if any differ it throws away the cached value and runs the lambda again. Anything you read inside the lambda that can change should be a key, otherwise you cache a stale result."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Without keys, the lambda runs exactly once per time the call site enters the composition.
  • With keys, the slot stores the keys plus the value. Changed key means recalculate and overwrite. The old value, if it implements RememberObserver, gets onForgotten.
  • Comparison is equals, so a List key compares element by element (cost grows with size) and a class without equals compares by identity (new instance each pass means recalculation every pass).
  • rememberSaveable takes the same idea but names the parameter inputs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun ContactList(contacts: List<Contact>, comparator: Comparator<Contact>) {
    // Both inputs read inside the lambda are keys
    val sorted = remember(contacts, comparator) { contacts.sortedWith(comparator) }
    LazyColumn { items(sorted, key = { it.id }) { ContactRow(it) } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting a key: result is stale when the input changes.
  • Keying on a lambda or fresh object created in the parent each pass: recalculates every time and the cache is useless.
  • Passing a large list as key for a trivial calculation: the equals can cost more than the calculation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does remember(key) reset when key goes A to B to A? → Yes, it recalculates on each change; it does not keep a history.
  2. Difference from LaunchedEffect(key)? → Both restart on key change; remember recomputes synchronously during composition, the effect runs after composition in a coroutine.
  3. How do you reset rememberSaveable state when an ID changes? → Pass the ID as an input, rememberSaveable(userId) { ... }.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "keys invalidate the cache." Senior: states equality is equals, weighs the cost of comparing big keys, and uses keys deliberately to scope state lifetime (reset per item or per user).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A profile screen kept the previous user's draft bio after switching accounts because the draft state had no userId key.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between remember and rememberSaveable, and exactly what does rememberSaveable survive?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic, but candidates overclaim ("survives everything") and miss the user-dismissal case.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "remember survives recomposition only. rememberSaveable additionally survives activity recreation, such as rotation, and system-initiated process death, because it writes the value into saved instance state. It does not survive the user swiping the app away or finishing the activity. Values must be Bundle-compatible or use a custom Saver."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• rememberSaveable is a wrapper around remember. It registers a value provider with the SaveableStateRegistry, which the host (ComponentActivity, Fragment, navigation) ties to onSaveInstanceState. On recreation the restored value is passed back instead of running the init lambda.
  • Config change: composition destroyed, activity recreated, state restored from the saved Bundle.
  • System-initiated process death: Bundle is persisted by the system and restored when the user returns.
  • User dismissal (swipe from recents, back out of the root): saved state is discarded. That is by design.
  • The Bundle is shared with everything else saving state and is size limited (see the TransactionTooLarge incident question).
Event remember rememberSaveable ViewModel
Recomposition Yes Yes Yes
Rotation No Yes Yes
System process death No Yes No (needs SavedStateHandle)
User dismisses No No No

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Search() {
    var query by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") } // String is Bundle-safe
    OutlinedTextField(value = query, onValueChange = { query = it })
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saving big lists or bitmaps.
  • Assuming it survives the user closing the app.
  • Using it for screen data that should be reloaded from the data layer.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the ViewModel survive process death? → No. Use SavedStateHandle for small UI state.
  2. What goes wrong with a non-Parcelable data class? → It throws at save time (not at creation) because it cannot be put in a Bundle; give it a Saver or @Parcelize.
  3. How do you test it? → StateRestorationTester for recreation, and adb shell am kill or "Don't keep activities" for process death.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "survives rotation." Senior: lists the three loss events, ties it to SaveableStateRegistry, and says what belongs here (transient UI input, selection IDs) versus what belongs in the data layer.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Forms that kept text across rotation in QA still lost it for users returning after the OS killed the process, because the state was in a ViewModel only.

questions.promptHtml: What is state hoisting in Compose, and how do you decide how far up to hoist?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the base pattern behind reusable, testable composables and unidirectional data flow.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Hoisting moves state out of a composable into its caller, replacing the internal variable with a value parameter and an onValueChange event. State flows down, events flow up. I hoist to at least the lowest common ancestor of everything that reads it, and at least as high as the highest place that writes it, and if two states change on the same event they go up together."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• A stateful composable owns state with remember. A stateless one takes state and events as parameters. Libraries usually offer both (stateful convenience wrapper over a stateless core).
  • Benefits per the official docs: single source of truth, encapsulated writes, shareable, interceptable (the caller can reject or transform an event), decoupled storage (can move to a ViewModel later).
  • Do not hoist everything. Purely internal UI state (an animation toggle) can stay inside if nobody else needs it. Under-hoisting breaks UDF; over-hoisting causes parameter drilling and recompositions of big subtrees.
HelloScreen  (owns name)
  | name, onNameChange
  v
HelloContent (stateless)  -- event --> HelloScreen updates name

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun HelloScreen() {
    var name by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") }
    HelloContent(name = name, onNameChange = { name = it })
}

@Composable
fun HelloContent(name: String, onNameChange: (String) -> Unit) {
    OutlinedTextField(value = name, onValueChange = onNameChange)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Duplicating state (child keeps a copy, parent keeps another) so they drift.
  • Passing the whole ViewModel down instead of state and lambdas.
  • Hoisting to the Activity "just in case".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not wrapper classes holding all state and events? → Official guidance prefers explicit parameters: it keeps each composable's responsibilities visible and passes only what is needed.
  2. What does "interceptable" mean? → Parent can validate or ignore onValueChange (e.g. max length) before writing.
  3. Hoisting vs recomposition cost? → Writing hoisted state invalidates readers at the owner; read it lazily (lambda) to narrow the invalidated scope when it changes every frame.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "pass value and callback." Senior: applies the lowest-common-ancestor and highest-writer rules, distinguishes UI-element state from screen state, and knows when not to hoist.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reusable chip component owned its own selected state, so two screens showing the same filter disagreed; hoisting made one source of truth.

questions.promptHtml: How does rememberSaveable decide what it can save, and when do you use @Parcelize, listSaver, mapSaver or a custom Saver?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the Bundle constraint and can persist custom state holders without crashing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "By default it uses an auto saver that accepts anything a Bundle accepts: primitives, Strings, Parcelable, Serializable and so on. For other types I either add @Parcelize, or write a Saver. listSaver maps to a list by index, mapSaver to a map with keys so it survives field reordering. A custom Saver gives me full control, for example to save only an ID."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• A Saver<Original, Saveable> has save and restore. Saveable must itself be Bundle-compatible. Returning null from save means "skip".
  • For MutableState<T> use the overload rememberSaveable(stateSaver = ...) { mutableStateOf(..) }: the saver is for T, not the state wrapper.
  • mapSaver key names make restore tolerant to adding fields (missing key is a null you handle). listSaver is shorter but positional: reordering fields silently breaks old saved data (matters only across process death within one install, since saved state does not survive app updates in practice; still fragile for review).
  • Choose by data: small Parcelable is simplest; @Parcelize ties your model to Android; a Saver keeps the model pure Kotlin.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class City(val name: String, val country: String)

val CitySaver = listSaver<City, Any>(
    save = { listOf(it.name, it.country) },
    restore = { City(it[0] as String, it[1] as String) }
)

@Composable
fun CityPicker() {
    var city by rememberSaveable(stateSaver = CitySaver) {
        mutableStateOf(City("Madrid", "Spain"))
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saving a collection of large objects: Bundle bloat.
  • Casting in restore without handling absent keys (mapSaver).
  • Putting a non-saveable object (lambda, Context) in the state: crashes at save time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does it blow up if the type is not saveable? → When the registry checks canBeSaved at save time, with an IllegalArgumentException naming the type.
  2. How do you save a mutableStateListOf? → Needs a custom Saver (e.g. listSaver over the items) or keep IDs only; verify per release as library helpers evolved.
  3. Do Savers run on the main thread? → Yes, during onSaveInstanceState, so keep them cheap.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use Parcelize." Senior: explains the stateSaver overload, saves identifiers not payloads, picks mapSaver for resilience, and tests restoration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash cluster "cannot be saved using the current SaveableStateRegistry" came from a rememberSaveable holding a data class with a lambda field.

questions.contextHtml:
A product-search screen (≈2M DAU) shows filtered results. QA reports: "after tapping a category chip the list does not change until I rotate the phone." No crash, no logs. The code:

@Composable
fun ResultsList(products: List<Product>, category: String, onClick: (Product) -> Unit) {
    val filtered = remember { products.filter { it.category == category } }
    LazyColumn {
        items(filtered, key = { it.id }) { ProductRow(it, onClick) }
    }
}

The ViewModel emits a new products list on every search and category on every chip tap. A teammate suspects the StateFlow is not emitting.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why rotation "fixes" it, and say how you would prevent this class of bug.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The flow is probably conflated, add distinctUntilChanged or call notifyDataSetChanged equivalent." They chase the data layer and never inspect the remember call.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does ResultsList recompose when the chip is tapped (Layout Inspector counts)? That separates "stale cache" from "no recomposition". Does the parent pass new arguments? Does it reproduce on first search too? Is it only after the second input change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: One-line hotfix: add the inputs as keys, remember(products, category).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) remember without keys caches the first filter result; (b) flow not emitting; (c) list is mutated in place; (d) key collision in items.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector shows ResultsList recomposing but filtered unchanged; add a temporary log inside the remember lambda: it prints once. Log in the ViewModel collector shows emissions arrive.
  5. Root cause: remember with no keys runs the lambda once per entry into composition. Recomposition re-reads the slot, so the old filtered list is returned although products and category parameters changed. Rotation recreates the composition, the lambda runs again with current inputs, which is why it "fixes" it.
  6. Fix: Short-term: remember(products, category) { ... }. Long-term: move the filter into the ViewModel (combine flows) and expose the filtered list so the composable has nothing to cache.
  7. Prevention: Review rule: every non-constant read inside remember is a key; lint/detekt rule where available (verify); a UI test that changes inputs and asserts the list.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not remove remember blindly (filtering 5k items per frame in scroll recompositions is wasteful). Not key by a large list if the filter is cheap; compare cost of equals against recompute.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• If products is a 20k-item list, is keying on it fine? → equals is O(n) per recomposition; prefer doing the work in the ViewModel or keying by a version/hash exposed by the state.
  • Would derivedStateOf fix it? → Only if inputs were State objects read inside the block; with plain parameters, keys are the right tool.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A catalog screen in a composite team showed last session's filter after login switch. The cache lived at the right level but never had the user ID as key; the fix was two characters and a regression test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the flow or adds forced recomposition hacks.
  • Hire: Finds missing keys, explains rotation behavior, fixes it.
  • Strong hire: Also discusses equals cost, moving the work to the ViewModel, and a review/test guard.

questions.promptHtml: When does derivedStateOf help, and when is it pure overhead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most over-used API in Compose codebases; seniors know it is a dampener, not a "computed property".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "derivedStateOf makes a State computed from other state objects. It only notifies its readers when the computed result changes, so it helps when inputs change much more often than the output, like scroll index to a boolean 'show button'. If the output changes as often as the inputs, like a full name from first and last, it is extra bookkeeping and I should just compute it inline."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The calculation block reads snapshot states. The runtime tracks those reads as dependencies. When any dependency changes, the derived state is marked dirty, but readers are invalidated only if the new result differs from the old (equality policy, structural by default).
  • Without it, a composable reading listState.firstVisibleItemIndex directly recomposes on every index change (0,1,2,3...). With derivedStateOf { index > 0 } it recomposes only when the boolean flips.
  • It is not free: it allocates a derived state object and tracks dependencies. The official guidance calls it expensive and to use it only to avoid unnecessary recomposition.
  • It does not stop the parent from recomposing when the composable's own parameters change. It only dampens state reads.
  • Newer runtimes: the Compose docs describe computedStateOf for Compose Runtime 1.13+ as a lighter option that re-evaluates on each read without caching; verify availability and stability against your BOM before relying on it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val listState = rememberLazyListState()
val showButton by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } }

// Anti-pattern: output changes as often as inputs
var first by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
var last by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
val full = "$first $last"   // correct, no derivedStateOf

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping derivedStateOf in remember(listState.firstVisibleItemIndex) keys: recreates it on every change and defeats it (see the dedicated scenario).
  • Using it for values derived from plain parameters (no snapshot state read inside, so nothing to track).
  • Forgetting remember, so a new derived state is created each pass.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How is it different from remember(key)? → remember(key) recomputes when a parameter changes; derivedStateOf tracks snapshot state reads and filters invalidation by result.
  2. Difference from snapshotFlow? → derivedStateOf yields a State for composition; snapshotFlow yields a cold Flow for effects.
  3. Does it affect the recomposition scope that created it? → The scope reads the derived State, so it is invalidated only on result change; but the scope still recomposes for other reasons.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "caches computed values." Senior: "it throttles invalidation; use only with a big input-to-output change-rate gap, and consider deferring the read to layout/draw instead."

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed screen wrapped trivial string concatenations in derivedStateOf, adding allocations to every row bind; removing them cut allocations without any UI change.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between collectAsState and collectAsStateWithLifecycle, and why does it matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests lifecycle awareness in Compose, battery, and wasted upstream work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "collectAsState collects as long as the composable is in the composition. When the app is backgrounded the Activity stops but the composition is still alive, so collection and any upstream work continue. collectAsStateWithLifecycle collects only while the lifecycle is at least STARTED by default and cancels collection below that, so upstream producers can stop. On Android that is the right default."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Both convert a Flow into State that composition can read. For a StateFlow the initial value is value; for a plain Flow you must supply initialValue.
  • collectAsStateWithLifecycle lives in lifecycle-runtime-compose (docs: 2.6.0-beta01 or newer) and uses repeatOnLifecycle semantics with minActiveState = STARTED by default.
  • It matters most when the upstream is expensive: stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5_000)) in the ViewModel stops upstream 5 seconds after the last collector leaves. If the UI keeps collecting in background, upstream never stops.
  • collectAsState remains right for platform-agnostic (KMP) code.
Activity STOPPED, composition alive
collectAsState           -> still collecting, upstream hot
collectAsStateWithLifecycle -> collection cancelled, WhileSubscribed timer starts

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun FeedScreen(vm: FeedViewModel = viewModel()) {
    val state by vm.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    FeedContent(state)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using collectAsState and wondering why location or socket flows run in background.
  • Collecting in LaunchedEffect without repeatOnLifecycle, same leak.
  • Assuming it stops events being lost: for one-off events use a design that does not drop (A4).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a 5s WhileSubscribed timeout? → Survives rotation without restarting upstream, stops it when the user really leaves.
  2. Can you change the threshold? → Yes, minActiveState (e.g. RESUMED).
  3. What about LiveData? → observeAsState, which follows the lifecycle owner via LiveData itself.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "lifecycle-aware version." Senior: ties it to WhileSubscribed, measures upstream work stopping in background, and notes KMP trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tracking screen kept GPS updates alive while backgrounded for hours until collection was moved to collectAsStateWithLifecycle.

questions.promptHtml: When would you create a plain state holder class in Compose instead of keeping state in composables or a ViewModel?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who stuff everything in the ViewModel from those who place state by its logic type.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "When a composable accumulates several pieces of UI-element state plus UI logic, like scroll position and 'jump to bottom' behavior, I move them into a plain class created with remember through a rememberXState function. It follows the composition lifecycle, can take Compose types like LazyListState, and is easy to test. Business logic and data access stay in the ViewModel."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Official guidance: composables own state when logic is simple; a plain state holder when UI logic grows; a ViewModel (screen-level holder) when business logic or data layers are involved.
  • Plain holders are annotated @Stable when appropriate, expose observable properties backed by mutableStateOf, and are built with remember(keys) so a changed input (window size class) recreates them.
  • If they must survive recreation, supply a Saver and use rememberSaveable.
  • A ViewModel outlives the composition, so putting Compose UI-element state there needs care: some state methods are suspend functions needing a MonotonicFrameClock (see the hoisting-in-ViewModel question).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Stable
class SearchBarState(initialQuery: String = "") {
    var query by mutableStateOf(initialQuery)
        private set
    val isActive get() = query.isNotBlank()
    fun onQueryChange(new: String) { query = new.take(80) }

    companion object {
        val Saver = Saver<SearchBarState, String>(
            save = { it.query },
            restore = { SearchBarState(it) }
        )
    }
}

@Composable
fun rememberSearchBarState(): SearchBarState =
    rememberSaveable(saver = SearchBarState.Saver) { SearchBarState() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Holding a Context or NavController in a holder that outlives it.
  • Putting repository calls in the plain holder.
  • Forgetting a Saver so state is lost on rotation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not always a ViewModel? → Lifetime mismatch and testability for pure UI logic; also ViewModels are scoped to an owner, not a composable instance.
  2. How to share between two screens? → Hoist above both, or ViewModel at a shared navigation scope.
  3. Is @Stable required? → It is a promise to the compiler; correct annotation lets skipping work for the holder as a parameter (see S1).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ViewModel for everything." Senior: splits UI logic from business logic and chooses lifetime on purpose.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard's ViewModel held LazyListState and crashed with "MonotonicFrameClock not available" when animating scrolls from viewModelScope.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app (single Activity, 4M DAU) ships a release where the article list screen stores the loaded page in rememberSaveable:

var articles by rememberSaveable(stateSaver = ArticleListSaver) { mutableStateOf(emptyList<Article>()) }

Each Article serializes to ~6 KB including HTML summary; the user can scroll up to 200 items. Crash reporting after rollout shows:

java.lang.RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1048364 bytes
  at android.app.servertransaction.ActivityTransactionItem...

Rate: 0.9% of sessions on Android 9-12, mostly right after pressing Home. Rotation works fine in QA with 20 items. The team suspects a flaky OEM and a Binder bug.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Catch the exception" or "compress the parcel". Treats it as OEM noise.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How big is the whole saved Bundle per Activity (instrument with Bundle size logging in debug)? Does the crash correlate with list length? Which Android versions (behavior of when saved state is sent differs)? What other state also lands in the same Bundle (navigation, other screens)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Staged rollout halt; server-side flag or hotfix that stops saving the list (return null from the saver), so the crash stops while the proper fix lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Bundle over the ~1 MB shared binder transaction limit (200 × 6 KB = 1.2 MB, plus other state); (b) another screen's large state; (c) OEM-specific Binder issue (red herring, ruled out by math).
  4. How I'd verify each: Math: 200 × 6 KB ≈ 1.2 MB > ~1 MB limit (commonly cited, verify per version). Reproduce by scrolling to 200 items, pressing Home on an Android 9-12 device, and checking logcat. Measure with Parcel.obtain().dataSize() on the saved Bundle in debug.
  5. Root cause: The Bundle written at onSaveInstanceState is sent to the system server over Binder with a roughly 1 MB shared buffer, so a large list exceeds it. QA lists were small, so it was invisible.
  6. Fix: Short term: stop saving the list. Long term: save only minimum state (IDs, query, scroll position via rememberLazyListState) and reload from the data layer (Room/network cache), per the official guidance to store minimal keys.
  7. Prevention: Test with large datasets and "Don't keep activities"; add a debug assertion for saved-state size; code review rule: no collections of domain objects in rememberSaveable or SavedStateHandle.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not shrink the Article payload to squeeze under the limit (still fragile); not catch the exception (it happens in framework code). Cost: after process death the list reloads, which is acceptable if cached.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if a PM insists the list must be restored instantly? → Cache pages in Room and restore from there with the saved scroll ID.
  • Would moving it to the ViewModel solve it? → For rotation yes, process death no, and ViewModel is not size limited by Binder; restoration comes from the repository.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found that three independent screens each saved "just 200 KB"; none crashed alone, the shared Activity Bundle crossed the limit only when users deep-linked through all of them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Calls it an OEM bug or catches the exception.
  • Hire: Identifies the Bundle size limit, removes large state from saveable.
  • Strong hire: Does the math, proposes the ID-plus-reload design, and adds a size guard and test.

questions.promptHtml: How does snapshotFlow work, and how does it differ from derivedStateOf and collectAsState?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of the bridge between snapshot state and coroutines/Flow.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "snapshotFlow turns snapshot state reads into a cold Flow. When collected, it runs the block in a snapshot, records which state objects were read, emits the result, then re-runs the block whenever one of those states is written and the new value differs from the last emission. It is the tool for reacting to Compose state from coroutines, such as analytics when scrolled past item 0. derivedStateOf is the opposite direction: state to state for composition."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Runs the block, records reads via a read observer, and on an applied write to any read state schedules re-evaluation. Emissions are conflated and de-duplicated by equals, like distinctUntilChanged.
  • Multiple writes inside one applied snapshot yield a single emission (intermediate values are not observed).
  • Because it is a cold flow it only observes while collected, typically in a LaunchedEffect keyed on the state holder.
  • It supports operators (debounce, filter, mapLatest), which derivedStateOf cannot.
API Direction Consumer Operators
derivedStateOf State to State Composition None
snapshotFlow State to Flow Coroutines All
collectAsState Flow to State Composition n/a

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun TrackScroll(listState: LazyListState, onPassedFirst: () -> Unit) {
    val current by rememberUpdatedState(onPassedFirst)
    LaunchedEffect(listState) {
        snapshotFlow { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 }
            .distinctUntilChanged()
            .filter { it }
            .collect { current() }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading non-snapshot values (plain vars) and expecting emissions.
  • Doing heavy work inside the block, which re-runs on each change.
  • Using it to compute a value for UI that derivedStateOf would do synchronously.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can a rapid pair of writes produce one emission? → Emission happens after the snapshot is applied; intermediate values inside it are invisible.
  2. How would you debounce a TextField for search? → snapshotFlow { query }.debounce(300).mapLatest { search(it) } in an effect.
  3. Is it equivalent to a MutableStateFlow? → No: it is cold and tied to snapshot reads.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "converts state to flow." Senior: explains read tracking, conflation, and chooses between it and derivedStateOf by consumer.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Search-as-you-type fired a request per keystroke until snapshotFlow with debounce replaced LaunchedEffect(query) restarts.

questions.promptHtml: What is a stale capture in Compose, and how do rememberUpdatedState and remember keys relate to it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Stale lambdas are a leading source of "it uses the old value" bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A lambda captures the values it saw when it was created. If that lambda is stored by remember or held by a long-running effect, it keeps the old values after recomposition. Fix by either adding the value as a key so the stored object is rebuilt, or by wrapping it with rememberUpdatedState so the long-lived consumer always reads the latest one without restarting."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• remember { { doThing(x) } } captures x at first composition only. Later x changes are invisible to that lambda.
  • LaunchedEffect(Unit) { delay(2000); onDone() } captures the first onDone. If the parent passes a new lambda later, the effect still calls the old one.
  • rememberUpdatedState(onDone) returns a State updated every composition; the effect reads current.value at call time, so it uses the latest. Choose a key (restart effect) when a restart is meaningful, rememberUpdatedState when it is not (e.g. a timer).
  • Cross-reference: effect semantics are in E1.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Splash(onTimeout: () -> Unit) {
    val currentOnTimeout by rememberUpdatedState(onTimeout)
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        delay(1_500)
        currentOnTimeout()   // latest lambda, timer not restarted
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding the lambda as an effect key: timer restarts on every parent recomposition.
  • remember { { vm.save(text) } } capturing initial text.
  • Believing val locals are live references: they are values at capture time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does by rememberUpdatedState have a cost? → One state write per recomposition; trivial.
  2. Why not key on onTimeout and accept restarts? → Lambda identity may change each pass (non-memoized), restarting the effect constantly.
  3. Does strong skipping change this? → It memoizes lambdas that capture stable values, so identity changes less often, but do not rely on it for correctness (verify per compiler version, see S1).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use rememberUpdatedState in effects." Senior: explains the capture mechanics, the key-vs-updated-state trade-off, and where remember itself creates stale closures.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A save-on-exit callback captured an early draft value and wrote an empty draft on back press.

questions.promptHtml: How does remember and rememberSaveable state inside LazyColumn items behave as you scroll, reorder or rotate, and what do key and contentType change?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Item state "jumping" to the wrong row is a very common bug, and it comes straight from identity rules.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Inside a lazy item, remember state belongs to that item's composition slot. When the item scrolls off screen, its composition is disposed (or the slot is reused), and remember state is lost. With a stable key, Compose maps state to the key, so reordering moves state with the item, and rememberSaveable state is saved by key and restored on scroll back. Without keys the identity is the index, so state sticks to positions. contentType lets slots be reused only between similar items."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Default key is the index. Insert at 0 and every item's position shifts, so its position-keyed state now belongs to a different item.
  • With key = { it.id }, the slot follows the data across moves and also gets rememberSaveable restoration. Lazy layouts save item state through the saveable registry keyed by your key, so keys must be Bundle-saveable (Int, Long, String; official guidance says never use index or hashCode()).
  • remember state does not survive scrolling away unless you hoist it (state map by id in the holder or ViewModel). rememberSaveable survives scroll-out via the registry, and rotation too.
  • contentType allows reuse of a disposed item's slot structure for the next item of that type, reducing composition cost; reuse still re-runs the item lambda with new data.
Unkeyed, expanded[2] = true         Keyed by id
insert new item at 0                insert new item at 0
position 2 now shows a different    state follows item id=7 to position 3
item, still "expanded"

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
LazyColumn {
    items(items = notes, key = { it.id }, contentType = { it.type }) { note ->
        var expanded by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) } // restored per key
        NoteRow(note, expanded, onToggle = { expanded = !expanded })
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Keys that are not unique: crash ("Key was already used").
  • Using hashCode() or a non-Bundle-safe key type.
  • Keeping expand state in remember and expecting it after scroll.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens with duplicate keys? → Runtime crash.
  2. Where do you put state that must survive a data refresh? → Hoist into a holder keyed by id, not into the row.
  3. Does contentType change state identity? → No, only slot reuse; state is still keyed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "add keys for performance." Senior: ties keys to state identity and saveable restoration and chooses where hoisted per-item state lives. (Full lazy-list internals are in Z1.)

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An order list showed "expanded" rows for the wrong orders after a new order arrived at the top because items had no keys.

questions.contextHtml:
A messaging app (low-end device mix, 35% under 3 GB RAM) has a "scroll to bottom" FAB. Janky scroll reported on a 5k-message thread: p95 frame time 38 ms vs 14 ms on the previous screen. Layout Inspector shows Thread recomposing on every scroll frame. The code:

@Composable
fun Thread(messages: List<Message>) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()
    val showFab by remember(listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset) {
        derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 3 }
    }
    Box {
        LazyColumn(state = listState) { items(messages, key = { it.id }) { MessageRow(it) } }
        if (showFab) ScrollToBottomFab()
    }
}

The author says "we already use derivedStateOf, so it can't be this." A teammate blames MessageRow.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix and verify it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more remember, make Message @Immutable." Does not read the remember keys.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does MessageRow recompose per frame or only Thread? Debug or release build? Is the compiler stability report clean for Message? That separates three causes.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the remember keys (remember { derivedStateOf { ... } }) and ship as hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) remember keyed on a state value read in composition recreates the derived state and reads the scroll offset in composition each frame; (b) MessageRow unstable; (c) debug-build overhead; (d) FAB animation.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector recomposition counts: Thread increments per frame, rows do not (rows are keyed and skippable). A release build measured with Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric.
  5. Root cause: listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset is read in composition as a remember key, so Thread is invalidated every scroll pixel. The key changes, remember throws away the derived state and builds a new one, which defeats the dampening. The derived state would have been fine alone.
  6. Fix: val showFab by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 3 } }. The derived state reads state internally, so Thread is invalidated only when the boolean flips. Verify: recomposition count drops from per-frame to twice per long scroll.
  7. Prevention: Review rule: never pass the state read inside derivedStateOf as a remember key (the official docs call this out). Add a Macrobenchmark scroll test with a frame time threshold.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not remove derivedStateOf in favor of snapshotFlow; not "optimize" MessageRow first without evidence. On Compose runtime 1.13+ computedStateOf may fit this case better; verify before adopting.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the threshold depends on a parameter minIndex? → Add minIndex as a remember key: it is a parameter, changes rarely.
  • Would deferring the FAB read help further? → Yes: read via a lambda or graphicsLayer so only the FAB subtree is invalidated.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team had three screens copy-pasted from one wrong snippet; one Macrobenchmark with a jank budget caught all three after the fix.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Optimizes the row, ignores the keys.
  • Hire: Spots the key bug and fixes it.
  • Strong hire: Explains the invalidation mechanics, verifies with Layout Inspector and a benchmark, and adds a prevention rule.

questions.promptHtml: Explain identity in Compose. How do positional memoization, key() and movableContentOf affect where remember state lives?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It reveals whether you understand why state sticks to the wrong item and how to control it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Compose identifies a call by its position in the composition tree (a group key from the compiler plus order). remember state is attached to that position. If I render items in a loop, position equals index, so reordering moves data but not state. key(id) { ... } replaces positional identity with a value so state follows the id. movableContentOf goes further and lets a whole composition, including its state, move to a different parent."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The compiler generates a group around each call. In control flow, if branches get different groups, so toggling a branch drops the state of the removed branch.
  • Loops produce the same group repeatedly; the runtime disambiguates by call order. Insert at the front and every later call's state moves.
  • key(x) introduces a group keyed by x compared with equals; compose can match groups across reorders, preserve state, and move nodes instead of recreating them.
  • movableContentOf handles a case key cannot: the content moves between different parent composables (e.g. phone to tablet layout), keeping state and avoiding recreating nested views like a video player.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Column {
    for (task in tasks) {
        key(task.id) {            // state follows task.id, not index
            var done by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
            TaskRow(task, done) { done = it }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Non-unique key values in the same parent.
  • Using key with unstable values that change each pass (state reset).
  • Assuming remember state is tied to the data object.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. key in a lazy list vs key() composable? → Lazy key parameter feeds the item provider and saveable registry; key() is for ordinary composition.
  2. State when an if toggles false then true? → Dropped; use hoisting if it should persist.
  3. When use movableContentOf? → Layout changes that reparent expensive content; check API stability for your version (verify).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use keys in lists." Senior: explains groups and positional identity and picks between key, hoisting and movable content.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A drag-to-reorder to-do list kept checkmarks at their slots after reorder until each row was wrapped in key(task.id).

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout screen's coupon field was moved from local state into the ViewModel as part of a state-hoisting cleanup. After release, support tickets: "cursor jumps to the start when I type fast", "characters disappear on slow devices". Affects about 4% of users, mostly mid-range devices. The code:

// ViewModel
private val _coupon = MutableStateFlow("")
val coupon: StateFlow<String> = _coupon
fun onCouponChange(v: String) { viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) { _coupon.value = v.trim() } }

// UI
val coupon by vm.coupon.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
OutlinedTextField(value = coupon, onValueChange = vm::onCouponChange)

No crash logs. The team suspects the IME.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how would you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Revert to local state." Or blames the keyboard without a mechanism.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which devices and IMEs? Did the problem exist before the hoisting change? Is the update dispatched asynchronously? Any transformation on the string (the trim)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the field to local rememberSaveable state (behind flag), pushing the final value to the ViewModel on blur or submit.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) State update is asynchronous (Dispatchers.Default plus a StateFlow hop), so the TextField renders an old value while the IME has moved on; (b) trim() changes the text from what the IME proposed, shifting the selection; (c) IME bug; (d) recomposition delays on slow devices widen the gap.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add trace sections around onValueChange to render; reproduce with a throttled CPU and fast typing; log values at the IME callback vs rendered value.
  5. Root cause: A TextField's value must reflect the new text synchronously within the same frame as onValueChange. The async write breaks that contract, so the field briefly renders a stale string and the composition resets the editing state, losing characters and cursor position.
  6. Fix: Write state synchronously on the main thread: var coupon by mutableStateOf("") in the ViewModel or a main-thread MutableStateFlow update (_coupon.value = v with no dispatcher hop); apply trim when submitting, not on each key. For heavy validation use a separate derived flow. Newer foundation versions provide a TextFieldState-based BasicTextField, which avoids this class of bug (verify the version in your BOM).
  7. Prevention: Rule: text input state updates synchronously; add a UI test that types quickly with a test dispatcher; keep transformations in output, not input.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "debounce the input" (would worsen it); not hoist input state to the ViewModel when no business logic needs it (the docs say keep it closer to the UI if not needed).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does a synchronous StateFlow update fully avoid the issue? → Generally yes if written on the main thread in the callback, though MutableState is the simplest.
  • How do you validate server-side coupon codes? → Debounced flow off the state, separate from the displayed text.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team's refactor moved every field into async reducers; the fix was a rule that input state is always a synchronous main-thread write, results are async.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the IME.
  • Hire: Finds the async write breaking synchronous TextField state.
  • Strong hire: Fixes it, separates input from validation, and mentions TextFieldState options with a verify note.

questions.promptHtml: When should Compose UI-element state live in a ViewModel, and what are the pitfalls of hoisting UI-element state there?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests judgment: not "everything in the ViewModel", plus knowledge of the MonotonicFrameClock trap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Screen UI state, produced by business rules, belongs in the ViewModel. UI-element state belongs in the ViewModel only if business logic needs to read or write it, like a search box whose text drives repository queries. Otherwise keep it in the UI. The pitfall is Compose state holders with suspend animation methods, such as LazyListState.animateScrollToItem or DrawerState.close(): calling them from viewModelScope throws because there is no MonotonicFrameClock."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• ViewModel outlives composition (survives rotation) and lives outside it. viewModelScope has no frame clock, which animation-driven suspend functions need.
  • Fix: pass a composition-scoped CoroutineScope (from rememberCoroutineScope) from the UI, or switch context with withContext(uiScope.coroutineContext) per the official guidance; better, keep the animatable state in the UI and send only the business event to the ViewModel.
  • Surviving process death still requires SavedStateHandle; the ViewModel alone does not.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Bad: viewModelScope has no MonotonicFrameClock
fun onSent() = viewModelScope.launch { listState.animateScrollToItem(0) }

// Good: UI owns the scope
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
Input(onSent = { vm.send(it); scope.launch { listState.animateScrollToItem(0) } })

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing LazyListState in a ViewModel (and leaking composition references).
  • Passing the ViewModel down to children.
  • Treating the ViewModel as the persistence layer for UI input.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not pass the ViewModel to children? → Couples them, hurts previews/tests; pass state and lambdas.
  2. How to expose both screen state and events? → See A4 for UDF design.
  3. What if you need scroll position to survive process death? → rememberLazyListState already saves via rememberSaveable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ViewModel holds state." Senior: splits by logic type, avoids framework-clock traps, and keeps UI mechanics in the UI.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "scroll to latest after send" feature crashed in QA with the frame clock exception after moving the call into the ViewModel.

questions.promptHtml: What happens inside remember and what lifecycle callbacks does a remembered object get?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests depth: slot table, equality, RememberObserver and abandoned compositions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "remember calls rememberedValue() on the Composer's slot table at the current position. If the slot is empty or keys changed, it runs the calculation and updates the slot. If the stored object implements RememberObserver, it gets onRemembered after the composition is applied, onForgotten when it leaves, and onAbandoned if the composition was discarded before being applied. That is why you must never start work in the remember lambda itself."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Composition can be started, then thrown away (state changed mid-way, a higher priority recomposition, an exception). Anything with external effect created in the calculation lambda would have run but never be tracked, thus leaking. RememberObserver.onAbandoned exists for this: cleanup of an object that was created but never remembered.
  • onRemembered runs when the changes are applied: start things here. onForgotten when the slot is overwritten (keys changed) or the call leaves composition: stop things here.
  • Keys: stored and compared using equals with each pass. Composer.changed(value) is the underlying check; the compiler also inlines cheap skipping checks.
  • Practical consequence: use DisposableEffect/LaunchedEffect for side effects (see E1); use remember only for creation and pure setup. Official docs warn that remember should be for expensive calc or identity-preserving objects.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class PollingHandle : RememberObserver {
    override fun onRemembered() { /* start */ }
    override fun onForgotten() { /* stop */ }
    override fun onAbandoned() { /* never started, drop refs */ }
}

@Composable
fun rememberPolling(interval: Long): PollingHandle =
    remember(interval) { PollingHandle() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling registerListener or launching coroutines inside the remember lambda.
  • Expecting onForgotten to run on process kill: it does not.
  • Heavy construction in the lambda blocking the composition frame.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can a composition be abandoned? → Composition may be interrupted or discarded before apply.
  2. When is onForgotten called relative to disposal of effects? → On leaving, with effect disposals in the apply phase (order details: verify in source).
  3. Is remember allowed in non-composable code? → No, it requires a Composer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "caches value." Senior: knows the observer contract and why side effects belong in effects.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A leaked sensor listener appeared in LeakCanary because registration happened in a remember lambda that ran in abandoned compositions.

questions.contextHtml: A food-delivery checkout (6M DAU) has a multi-step form: address, notes, promo code, tip slider. Support sees "I came back from my banking app and everything was empty" in ~3% of checkout sessions, concentrated on devices with 3 GB RAM or less. QA cannot reproduce: rotation keeps everything. Code summary: all fields live in CheckoutViewModel as mutableStateOf; no SavedStateHandle; no rememberSaveable. Crash-free rate is fine (99.7%).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the cause and fix it without bloating state saving.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The ViewModel survives configuration changes so it must be a network issue." Misses process death entirely.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it correlate with leaving the app (banking/OTP app) and low RAM? Did the app start from the login screen after return, or from checkout (restored)? Which fields: all or only some? That distinguishes process death from a logout bug.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Persist the draft of the form to local storage (small) on each field commit so it can be re-read on open.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) system-initiated process death clears the ViewModel; (b) session expiry redirect; (c) back stack restored to a different destination; (d) state cleared by an explicit reset.
  4. How I'd verify each: Developer options "Don't keep activities", or adb shell am kill <pkg> after backgrounding, then relaunch from recents; check whether the screen is recreated with empty state. Telemetry: log "restored after process death" on Activity savedInstanceState != null with a fresh ViewModel.
  5. Root cause: ViewModels live in process memory. When the OS kills the backgrounded process, Android restores the Activity and navigation from saved instance state, but the ViewModel is new, so unsaved form state is gone.
  6. Fix: For small UI-element state (text, selected IDs, tip index) use SavedStateHandle (with saveable for Compose state, which the docs mark experimental) or rememberSaveable in the UI. For the cart (large, server-backed), save only the cart ID and reload. Do not store the whole cart in the Bundle.
  7. Prevention: Add process-death tests (StateRestorationTester for UI, instrumentation that kills and restores) and a checklist "what does this screen show after process death?"
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not move everything to rememberSaveable (Bundle limit, see the TransactionTooLarge question); not persist sensitive fields (card numbers, OTP) at all, even if technically possible; accept losing transient UI like an open dropdown.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should the promo code be saved? → Save it (small, user input), but revalidate server-side after restore.
  • How do you test it in CI? → Instrumentation with ActivityScenario.recreate() for config, and a process-kill scripted test on a device lab.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team shipped "state restoration" using Parcelable domain objects, which then crashed on updates; their redesign stored IDs and reloaded.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames network or session.
  • Hire: Identifies process death and uses SavedStateHandle/rememberSaveable.
  • Strong hire: Chooses the minimal state split, handles sensitive data, and has a test strategy.

questions.promptHtml: What goes wrong when you write a custom Saver for a state holder class with mutableStateOf fields, and how do you do it correctly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many people write Savers that save the wrapper, lose fields, or crash at save time.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A Saver converts the object to something Bundle-compatible and back. For a holder, I save the plain values of its state properties, not the MutableState wrappers, and restore by constructing a new holder from them. I keep it minimal, handle missing or malformed data on restore, and choose between listSaver, mapSaver and a custom Saver based on how stable the schema must be."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Saver<Original, Saveable>: SaverScope.save(value) returns the saveable; restore(saveable) returns Original? (null aborts restoration so the init lambda runs). Both run on the main thread during onSaveInstanceState and restore.
  • rememberSaveable(stateSaver = ...) { mutableStateOf(x) } wraps the state; the stateSaver is for x's type.
  • autoSaver is the default; it rejects types the registry cannot save by throwing at save time. Test with StateRestorationTester so failures show in CI.
  • Pitfalls: nesting saveables (use with(...) and save scope to delegate to another saver); capturing Context or listeners; saving derived data you can recompute; mutating the holder's constructor signature across versions.
  • Saving collections: element-by-element conversion, or save IDs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FilterState(category: String, minRating: Int) {
    var category by mutableStateOf(category)
    var minRating by mutableIntStateOf(minRating)

    companion object {
        val Saver: Saver<FilterState, *> = listSaver(
            save = { listOf(it.category, it.minRating) },
            restore = { FilterState(it[0] as String, it[1] as Int) }
        )
    }
}

@Composable
fun rememberFilterState() = rememberSaveable(saver = FilterState.Saver) {
    FilterState("all", 0)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning the MutableState itself from save.
  • Unsafe casts in restore that throw on schema drift.
  • Saving large lists or images.
  • Doing disk or heavy work in save.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does returning null from restore do? → The init lambda runs instead (fresh state).
  2. How do you verify? → StateRestorationTester.emulateSavedInstanceStateRestore().
  3. How is it different from @Parcelize? → Parcelize couples your model to Android and serializes all fields; a Saver lets you choose.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "implement save/restore." Senior: minimal payload, defensive restore, test coverage.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app crashed on first launch after an update because a listSaver index shifted between versions; the fix added mapSaver keys and null-safe restore.

questions.contextHtml:
A contacts screen (low-end device share 40%, lists up to 8,000 contacts) shows a sorted, grouped list and a search box. Profiling a Macrobenchmark scroll on a mid-tier device: median frame 11 ms but p99 32 ms, with a periodic 40 ms spike. Trace shows time in Intrinsics.areEqual and ArrayList.equals under ContactsScreen. The code:

@Composable
fun ContactsScreen(contacts: List<Contact>, query: String) {
    val grouped = remember(contacts, query) {
        contacts.filter { it.name.contains(query, ignoreCase = true) }
            .sortedBy { it.name }
            .groupBy { it.name.first().uppercaseChar() }
    }
    val total = remember(contacts) { contacts.size }
    // LazyColumn over grouped ...
}

contacts is a new List instance emitted by a Room query on each DB change; Contact is a data class.
questions.promptHtml: Why the spikes, and what would you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make Contact immutable and add derivedStateOf everywhere." Misses the cost of key equality and where the work should live.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How often does the list instance change? Does the content actually change, or does Room re-emit equal lists? Is the spike aligned with a DB invalidation? Release build measured?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop the total remember (the docs warn comparing a large collection as a key costs more than reading .size), read contacts.size directly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) key equals on an 8k list each recomposition; (b) filter/sort/group recomputed on every query keystroke and every re-emission; (c) Room re-emits equal data after unrelated table writes; (d) GC pressure from regrouping.
  4. How I'd verify each: System trace with custom trace sections around the lambda; count lambda runs versus recompositions; Room invalidation log; allocation profiler.
  5. Root cause: remember(contacts, query) compares contacts with equals, which is O(n) element-by-element over data classes, on every recomposition (including scroll-driven ones where the list is unchanged). When the DB re-emits an equal but new instance the compare walks all 8k elements, then recomputes the whole pipeline anyway when a single field differs.
  6. Fix: Move filter, sort and group off the UI thread into the ViewModel as a flow (combine(contactsFlow, queryFlow).mapLatest { ... }.flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) with distinctUntilChanged), expose the final grouped immutable structure, and have the composable just render. Short term: key by a cheap version (e.g. contacts.size plus a revision counter exposed by the ViewModel) rather than the list.
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark scroll test with a p99 budget; trace sections for heavy composition work; rule: no O(n) work or O(n) key in composition for lists above a few hundred items.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not cache by identity (===) blindly: a mutated list would be stale. Not debounce query by raising latency beyond ~100–150 ms without UX sign-off.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if query changes every keystroke? → mapLatest cancels old work, and compute on Dispatchers.Default.
  • Would derivedStateOf help? → Only if inputs are State; here the cost is key equality and in-composition work.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team measured that an innocuous remember(items) on 10k rows cost more per frame than the sort it was avoiding; moving the work to a flow removed both.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds more caching.
  • Hire: Identifies key equality cost and moves work to the ViewModel.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies, proposes versioned keys, tests with a benchmark.

questions.promptHtml: How does rememberSaveable interact with navigation (back stack entries, tabs) and what state do you lose when navigating away?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: People assume screen state is cleared on navigate; real behavior depends on the navigation library and whether the composable leaves the composition.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "When you navigate forward, the previous destination leaves the composition, so remember state is gone. rememberSaveable state is saved into the destination's saved state, and restored when you come back through the back stack. For bottom-nav tabs, whether it survives depends on saveState/restoreState options in the navigation call; with them it is restored. The ViewModel scoped to the back stack entry lives until the entry is popped."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Navigation Compose hosts each back stack entry with its own saveable state holder, so rememberSaveable inside a destination is saved when it leaves the composition and restored on return.
  • Popping the entry discards its saved state and its ViewModel (scoped to the entry). Tab switching with popUpTo(...) { saveState = true } plus restoreState = true keeps per-tab state; without them each tab starts fresh. Verify the exact behavior against your Navigation version.
  • Same-composition-position changes (e.g. AnimatedContent) are different: state follows composition position, not navigation.
  • Design: ephemeral UI state in rememberSaveable, screen data in a back-stack-scoped ViewModel, long-lived data in repositories.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
navController.navigate(route) {
    popUpTo(navController.graph.findStartDestination().id) { saveState = true }
    launchSingleTop = true
    restoreState = true   // restores rememberSaveable + back stack state for that tab
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming remember state survives when navigating forward and back.
  • Using the Activity-scoped ViewModel for screen state, so it never clears.
  • Forgetting restoreState for tabs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What clears a back stack entry's ViewModel? → Popping the entry.
  2. How is scroll position preserved on return? → rememberLazyListState uses rememberSaveable.
  3. What if the same composable is shown in two tabs? → Separate entries, separate state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "state is kept by the ViewModel." Senior: separates composition, saveable and ViewModel lifetimes per navigation operation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tabbed app reset search filters on every tab switch because tabs navigated without saveState.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing the "Orders" screen for a retail app (2M DAU, 20% on tablets). Elements: a search box, status filter chips, a list of 50–500 orders with expandable rows, a "select mode" with multi-selection and a bulk-cancel action, a pull-to-refresh state, and a snackbar after bulk-cancel with an Undo. Requirements: survive rotation and process death; list must keep scroll position; selection must clear on refresh; analytics for filter usage. A junior proposes putting everything in one OrdersViewModel state object.
questions.promptHtml: Where does each piece of state live and why?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Everything in the ViewModel." Or everything in rememberSaveable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is search server-side or local? Does cancel hit the network (business logic)? Should selection survive process death? Is the order list paginated? Answers change the split.
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a, this is a design; the first step is to classify state by logic type and lifetime.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: n/a. Alternatives: (a) single ViewModel state; (b) split by owner; (c) rememberSaveable for everything.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype with tests: rotation, process-kill, and fast-typing tests; check recomposition scope in Layout Inspector and Bundle size in debug.
  5. Root cause: n/a. Principle: place state at the lowest owner that satisfies lifetime and logic needs (official hoisting rules).
  6. Fix (my design):
    • OrdersViewModel (screen state): orders list, refresh status, bulk-cancel logic, undo events. Filter and search query live here because they drive repository queries (business logic), saved through SavedStateHandle (small strings/enums) for process death.
    • Composition (rememberSaveable): expanded row ids (a Set<Long> via a Saver), scroll position via rememberLazyListState.
    • Selection: ViewModel state but cleared on refresh; save selected ids only if product wants it after process death (I would not).
    • Snackbar: SnackbarHostState in the UI with rememberCoroutineScope; the ViewModel emits an event with undo token (UDF design details in A4).
    • Plain state holder OrdersScreenState for UI logic like "scroll to top when filter changes".
  7. Prevention: Document the state map in the PR; process-death test on the screen; Bundle size assertions.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not put the order list in SavedStateHandle (size); not store LazyListState in the ViewModel; not duplicate filter state in both UI and ViewModel. Single-ViewModel state would force the whole screen to recompose on tiny UI toggles, unless fields are read lazily.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tablet list-detail: where does selected order id live? → Hoist to the list-detail host (or navigation), saved via rememberSaveable.
  • Users complain scroll resets after refresh: why? → New list without stable keys; use keys.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team's single giant UiState recomposed the whole screen for every row expansion; splitting expansion into UI-level saveable state cut recomposition by an order of magnitude.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: One bucket for everything.
  • Hire: Splits UI state, screen state, and persisted state reasonably.
  • Strong hire: Justifies each placement by logic type and lifetime, handles process death size and stable keys, mentions tablet case.

questions.contextHtml: A ride-hailing app (5M DAU) wants to migrate 60 screens from collectAsState to collectAsStateWithLifecycle in a staged rollout. Telemetry before: battery team notes background CPU wakeups from the Home screen's driver-location flow; the ViewModel uses stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, ...). After migrating the first 10 screens (10% rollout) a regression appears: "map shows no cars for 1–2 s after returning from background" on 6% of resumes, and a new crash: IllegalStateException from a hot flow collected twice in a Fragment. Exit criteria: no extra cold-start cost, background wakeups reduced.
questions.promptHtml: How do you roll this out safely and what must change on the ViewModel side?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Find and replace across the codebase." Ignores SharingStarted and initial value behavior.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens' ViewModels use Eagerly or Lazily? What is the initial value? Is the map flow expensive to restart? Do any flows have side effects when collected (e.g. subscribing sockets)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the rollout flag; keep the migrated screens that show no regression; for the map screen keep upstream warm for a short window.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) After stop, collection ends and WhileSubscribed(5_000) stops upstream, so a return after 5s starts cold and shows empty initial state; (b) Eagerly upstream was hiding that cost before (upstream never stopped); (c) double collection from a duplicated collector; (d) initial value flicker due to StateFlow default.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log collection start/stop and first emission time; System trace of resume; battery profile for wakeups; checks per screen of stateIn parameters.
  5. Root cause: Before, upstream ran forever regardless of UI. collectAsStateWithLifecycle cancels collection below STARTED, so upstream becomes cold when the sharing strategy allows it. Return-from-background now pays restart latency, and a screen with an empty initial value shows empty state until the first emission.
  6. Fix: Change ViewModel flows to WhileSubscribed(5_000) (survives rotation, stops after 5s), seed state with last known driver positions (cache) so resume shows data immediately, and keep expensive hot sources (sockets) behind a repository that keeps last value. Remove the duplicated collector. Roll out screen-by-screen under a flag, comparing battery wakeups, resume time-to-first-data and crash rate.
  7. Prevention: Lint/detekt rule banning plain collectAsState in Android modules (verify tooling), a template for ViewModel stateIn, a startup/resume benchmark in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not leave Eagerly and just revert (loses the battery win); not set timeout large enough to defeat the purpose (a 5 s default matches the common recommendation but tune by measurement); not force STARTED vs RESUMED without checking multi-window cases.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What about screens in multi-window where the activity is visible but not RESUMED? → STARTED default still collects; RESUMED would pause, so keep STARTED.
  • Is repeatOnLifecycle equivalent? → Equivalent for non-Compose collection; use it in effects.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found their "bug" was the old behavior hiding 3 s of cold start; making the cache explicit improved both resume time and battery.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Mass replace without measurement.
  • Hire: Understands the interplay with WhileSubscribed and handles empty initial states.
  • Strong hire: Staged rollout with metrics, caches last value, covers multi-window and lint guard.
